questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless ulcer on the right hand with a black eschar and surrounding non-pitting oedema. Regional lymphadenopathy is present. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: Cutaneous anthrax caused by Bacillus anthracis presents as a painless papule that evolves into a vesicle and then a characteristic black eschar (malignant pustule) with surrounding non-pitting oedema. Occupation (farmer) is a classic clue.

questions.q: A 22-year-old immunocompromised patient presents with recurrent painful genital ulcers. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. Viral culture confirms the diagnosis. Which antiviral drug has the highest oral bioavailability among the options?
questions.exp: Valacyclovir (valyl ester of acyclovir) has oral bioavailability of 54-70%, much higher than acyclovir (15-30%). It is converted to acyclovir after absorption. Famciclovir (prodrug of penciclovir) has ~77% bioavailability but penciclovir oral is poor.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man from Bihar presents with a chronic plaque on the face. Biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation with Virchow cells (foam cells) containing bacilli. Slit skin smear shows a bacterial index of 5+. What type of leprosy does this patient have?
questions.exp: Lepromatous leprosy (LL) is characterized by a high bacterial index (5-6+), Virchow foam cells (lepra cells) on histology, diffuse skin involvement, weak CMI, and strong humoral response. BI of 5+ is consistent with LL or BL, but Virchow cells with BI 5+ points to LL.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with tense bullae on normal-appearing skin, predominantly in the flexural areas. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposits along the basement membrane zone. Which antibody is responsible?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid is characterized by IgG antibodies against BP180 (type XVII collagen, BPAG2) and BP230 (BPAG1). Tense bullae on normal/erythematous skin with linear IgG+C3 at BMZ on DIF is the classic presentation. Desmoglein antibodies are seen in pemphigus.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasias. ANA is positive with centromere pattern. Which internal organ complication is she most at risk for?
questions.exp: Anti-centromere antibody is associated with limited systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome). Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is the most serious complication in limited SSc with anti-centromere antibody. Renal crisis and pulmonary fibrosis are more common with diffuse SSc and anti-Scl-70.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male presents with an asymptomatic pearly papule with telangiectasias on the nose, present for 2 years. Dermoscopy shows arborizing vessels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin cancer. Nodular BCC presents as pearly/translucent papule with telangiectasias on sun-exposed areas (especially nose/face). Dermoscopy shows arborizing (tree-like) vessels, blue-grey ovoid nests, and spoke-wheel structures.

questions.q: A 28-year-old sexually active man presents with a painless indurated ulcer on the glans penis, with a clean base and firm non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Dark field microscopy is positive. What is the treatment of choice?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU single IM dose
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (Hunterian chancre) - painless indurated ulcer with non-tender regional lymphadenopathy. Treatment of choice is Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose. Doxycycline is used for penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.q: A 40-year-old diabetic presents with a rapidly spreading necrotizing infection of the scrotum with foul-smelling discharge and crepitus on palpation. What is this condition called?
questions.exp: Fournier's gangrene is a life-threatening polymicrobial necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum and genitalia. Risk factors include diabetes, immunosuppression. Crepitus indicates gas-forming organisms. Emergency surgical debridement with broad-spectrum antibiotics is essential.

questions.q: A 20-year-old presents with scaly pruritic plaques on the scalp with broken hair shafts. KOH mount shows hair shaft invasion with small spores outside the shaft. What is the type of tinea capitis?
questions.exp: Ectothrix tinea capitis shows spores arranged outside the hair shaft. Common organisms causing ectothrix: Microsporum canis, M. audouinii, T. verrucosum. Endothrix shows spores inside the shaft (T. tonsurans, T. violaceum). Fluorescence under Wood's lamp is seen in Microsporum infections.

questions.q: A patient with psoriasis develops warm, erythematous, tender joints and pitting of nails. X-ray shows pencil-in-cup deformity. Which HLA type is most associated with this arthropathy?
questions.exp: Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is seronegative and associated with HLA-B27, especially the axial/spondylitic form. Pencil-in-cup deformity on X-ray is characteristic of PsA. HLA-Cw6 is associated with cutaneous psoriasis itself. HLA-DR4 is associated with rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with honey-colored crusted lesions around the mouth and nares. Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. Which toxin is responsible for blister formation in the bullous variant?
questions.exp: Bullous impetigo is caused by Staphylococcus aureus phage group II producing exfoliative toxins A and B (epidermolytic toxins). These are serine proteases that cleave desmoglein-1, causing intraepidermal blistering within the stratum granulosum, same mechanism as SSSS.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with a butterfly-shaped rash on the face, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and arthralgia. ANA is 1:320 with anti-dsDNA positive. Which complement pathway is primarily activated in SLE?
questions.exp: In SLE, immune complexes (DNA-anti-dsDNA) activate the classical complement pathway via C1q binding to Fc portions of antibodies. Low C3 and C4 during active disease reflects complement consumption. C1q binding to apoptotic debris also links to disease pathogenesis.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man with chronic sun exposure develops a rapidly growing keratotic nodule on the back of hand over 6-8 weeks, with a central keratin-filled crater. It then begins to involute spontaneously. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Keratoacanthoma is a rapidly growing crateriform nodule with a central keratin plug that typically involutes within 4-6 months. It arises in sun-exposed areas of elderly patients and is histologically similar to SCC (considered a variant by some). The self-limiting nature is characteristic.

questions.q: A neonate develops widespread skin peeling with Nikolsky sign positive on day 4 of life. The skin resembles a scald. Blood cultures are negative. What is the causative toxin?
questions.exp: Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS) is caused by exfoliative toxins A and B from S. aureus. These toxins cleave desmoglein-1 at the stratum granulosum causing superficial blistering. Nikolsky sign is positive. Mucous membranes are spared (unlike TEN). Blood cultures are usually negative.

questions.q: A 35-year-old HIV-positive patient presents with painful, rapidly growing violaceous nodules on the lower limbs. Biopsy shows vascular proliferation with HHV-8 positive cells. CD4 count is 150. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: AIDS-associated Kaposi's sarcoma (HHV-8) - the primary treatment is ART (antiretroviral therapy) which improves immune function and often leads to regression. Liposomal doxorubicin is first-line for extensive/systemic KS. For localized KS in the setting of HIV, ART initiation is the cornerstone.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with pigmented macules on the face distributed in a V-shape on the cheeks, forehead, and upper lip. It worsens in summer. Wood's lamp examination shows enhancement of pigmentation. What layer of skin is affected?
questions.exp: Wood's lamp (365 nm UVA) enhances epidermal hyperpigmentation (appears more distinct/darker) but dermal pigmentation does not enhance. Melasma commonly has epidermal type which shows enhancement. This distinction helps guide treatment - epidermal type responds better to topical therapies.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in a dermatomal distribution on the left thorax, preceded by burning pain for 3 days. He is otherwise healthy. What is the mechanism of latency of the causative virus?
opts: Episomal latency in dorsal root ganglion neurons
questions.exp: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) becomes latent in dorsal root ganglia (cranial nerve ganglia for facial/ophthalmic distribution) as episomal DNA within neurons. Reactivation causes herpes zoster. HIV integration into host genome is seen with retroviruses like HIV.

questions.q: A patient with leprosy on MDT develops sudden appearance of tender erythematous nodules on the face and limbs with fever and arthralgia. ESR is elevated. Histology shows neutrophilic infiltrate in the dermis. What is this reaction?
questions.exp: Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL) or Type 2 lepra reaction occurs in BL/LL leprosy. It is immune-complex mediated (Type III hypersensitivity), presenting with tender erythematous nodules, fever, and systemic features. Histology shows neutrophilic infiltrate. Treated with thalidomide or prednisolone.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with a solitary, well-defined, pearly white plaque with a rough surface on the vermillion border of the lip. He smokes heavily. Biopsy shows dysplastic epithelial changes without invasion. What is this condition?
questions.exp: Actinic cheilitis (actinic keratosis of the lip) affects the lower lip predominantly due to sun exposure. It presents as scaly, thickened plaques on the vermillion border with blurring of the vermillion-skin junction. Heavy smoking is a risk factor. It is a premalignant condition for SCC.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with erythematous, scaly plaques in the axillae and groin that fluoresce coral red under Wood's lamp. Which organism is responsible and what antibiotic is used?
questions.exp: Erythrasma is caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum (gram-positive rod). It produces porphyrins that fluoresce coral red/brick red under Wood's lamp. It affects intertriginous areas. Treatment is oral erythromycin or topical fusidic acid/clindamycin.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis presents with palpable purpura on the lower limbs. Biopsy shows neutrophilic infiltrate around small blood vessels with nuclear dust (leukocytoclasis) and fibrinoid necrosis. What type of vasculitis is this?
questions.exp: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV) is the most common form of cutaneous vasculitis. Hallmark is neutrophilic infiltrate with nuclear dust (leukocytoclasis), fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls, and RBC extravasation. Palpable purpura on dependent areas is classic. Associated with RA, infections, drugs.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with multiple flesh-colored papules on the penile shaft and coronal sulcus. These are asymptomatic, and his partner has no lesions. Aceto-white test is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Pearly penile papules (PPP) are a normal anatomical variant - dome-shaped papules arranged in rows on the corona/coronal sulcus. They are NOT sexually transmitted, aceto-white test is negative (HPV-associated condylomata are aceto-white positive). No treatment required.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with thinning of hair on the crown with preservation of the frontal hairline. Pull test is negative. Dermoscopy shows miniaturization of hair follicles. What is the inheritance pattern?
questions.exp: Female pattern hair loss (FPHL)/Androgenetic alopecia follows autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance and is polygenic. It is androgen-dependent (5-alpha reductase converts testosterone to DHT). Ludwig classification describes severity. Minoxidil is first-line treatment.

questions.q: A neonate presents with widespread ichthyosis, ectropion, eclabium, and a collodion membrane at birth. The child later develops plate-like scales. Gene mutation involves transglutaminase-1. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Lamellar ichthyosis (autosomal recessive) classically presents as collodion baby. Mutations in TGM1 (transglutaminase-1) are the most common cause. Characterized by large, plate-like brown scales over the entire body with ectropion and eclabium. Epidermolytic ichthyosis involves keratin 1/10 mutations.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man develops severe widespread erythema and epidermal detachment affecting >30% BSA following sulfonamide therapy. Nikolsky sign is positive. Mucous membranes are involved. Which pathomechanism is primarily responsible?
opts: Cytotoxic CD8+ T cell-mediated keratinocyte apoptosis
questions.exp: Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) is primarily mediated by drug-specific CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes that induce keratinocyte apoptosis via granulysin (perforin-independent pathway) and FasL. Granulysin is now considered the key mediator. Sulfonamides, allopurinol, anticonvulsants are common causes.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with hypopigmented macules on the trunk after summer. KOH mount shows spaghetti and meatballs appearance. She says the lesions become more noticeable after tanning. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor (tinea versicolor) is caused by Malassezia furfur (Pityrosporum ovale). KOH mount shows short hyphae and round yeast cells ('spaghetti and meatballs'). Hypopigmentation occurs because Malassezia produces azelaic acid that inhibits tyrosinase. More noticeable post-tanning as surrounding skin darkens.

questions.q: A dermatology resident performs a patch test on a patient suspected of allergic contact dermatitis. The reading is done at 48 and 96 hours. A reaction shows erythema with papules and vesicles at the test site at 96 hours. What type of hypersensitivity is this?
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) and patch test reactions are classic Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity mediated by sensitized T lymphocytes (CD4+ Th1). Reaction peaks at 48-72 hours. The sensitization phase involves Langerhans cells presenting hapten-protein conjugates to T cells in lymph nodes.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male smoker presents with painful, punched-out ulcers on the gaiter area (lower legs) with a violaceous, undermined edge. The ulcers first appeared as tender nodules that broke down. Which pathological process underlies this condition?
questions.exp: Pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) is a neutrophilic dermatosis characterized by pathergy (lesions develop/worsen at sites of trauma). Pathergy is the hallmark - minor trauma initiates severe ulceration. Begins as painful nodule/pustule evolving to ulcer with violaceous undermined edges. Associated with IBD, RA, haematological malignancies.

questions.q: A 55-year-old female presents with diffuse non-scarring alopecia. TSH is elevated. Which hair cycle phase is predominantly affected in hypothyroid-induced hair loss?
questions.exp: Hypothyroidism causes telogen effluvium - premature shift of hairs from anagen to telogen phase, causing diffuse shedding. Thyroid hormones regulate hair cycle by prolonging anagen. Anagen effluvium (sudden loss) occurs with chemotherapy/radiation affecting rapidly dividing matrix cells. TSH should be checked in diffuse hair loss.

questions.q: During a PUVA (psoralen + UVA) treatment session for psoriasis, the mechanism of action involves DNA cross-linking. 8-methoxypsoralen intercalates into DNA and forms cyclobutane adducts with pyrimidine bases upon UVA activation. Which cell type is primarily targeted to achieve therapeutic effect?
questions.exp: PUVA therapy targets hyperproliferating keratinocytes (reducing excessive proliferation in psoriasis) and T lymphocytes (immunomodulation). Psoralen intercalates into DNA; UVA activation forms monofunctional and bifunctional adducts with thymine, inhibiting DNA replication and causing apoptosis of pathogenic cells.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman develops drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) following carbamazepine. Labs show eosinophilia, elevated liver enzymes, and atypical lymphocytes. Which virus is reactivated in DRESS syndrome?
questions.exp: DRESS (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms) / DiHS is characteristically associated with reactivation of Human Herpesvirus-6 (HHV-6), followed by HHV-7, EBV and CMV. Sequential herpesvirus reactivation is a hallmark. Aromatic anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) and allopurinol are common triggers.
